name: Self-persuasion
statement: Arguments people produce themselves are said to change their own attitudes and behaviour more than the same arguments handed to them.
meaning: The claim is about who produced the argument, not about what the argument says. Someone asked why a rule matters writes the case for it, and the case is then their own. Lemmen and colleagues state the premise as the motivation to act coming from within the person, citing Aronson. Cognitive dissonance, entry no. 24, is one proposed reason the procedure works rather than the procedure itself. Effort justification, entry no. 200, revalues what effort bought, while this revalues a position the person argued. So the testable part is a comparison, and a study of it needs a condition in which somebody else supplies the arguments.

origin.who: Irving L. Janis and Bert T. King
origin.where: The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
origin.note: The paper is titled "The influence of role playing on opinion change" and ran at 49(2), 211-218. It was read in full from the Internet Archive's scan of the 1954 volume. Ninety male college students sat in threes, each giving one of three prepared talks as a sincere advocate and listening while the other two gave theirs. Active speakers lowered their estimates further than passive listeners on two of the three topics, at p = .01 on the sizable-change measure. On the third topic, a cure for the common cold, the two groups moved about the same. The name self-persuasion belongs to Elliot Aronson's 1999 article in American Psychologist, 54(11), 875-884, which is closed.

evidence: King and Janis tested the improvisation account two years later, and that paper was read from the Internet Archive's scan of the 1956 volume. Thirty-two students gave a talk on military service from memory, 23 read the same script aloud, and 20 read it silently. The improvisers shifted further than the script readers on a combined index of five opinion items, p = .01, and further than the silent readers, p = .03. The script readers differed from the silent readers on no item, and ran the other way on the combined index, p > .30. They also rated their own performance more favourably, which rules out satisfaction as the reason. Greenwald and Albert had students improvise arguments on general against specialised undergraduate education, then copy out another student's arguments for the other side. Of 198 recruited, 181 were analysed. Opinions moved towards the side each student had been assigned at random, F(1, 177) = 7.42, p < .01. Own arguments were recalled far better than the other student's, F(1, 177) = 168.10, p < .001, and were rated more original, t(180) = 4.31, p < .001. Lemmen, Keizer, Bouman and Steg ran the comparison at Apenheul, a Dutch primate park. Signs at the entrance to the free-ranging enclosure either carried three arguments for not luring the squirrel monkeys, or asked visitors why they should not lure them, or carried both, or said nothing. Three observers dressed as visitors watched a marked area of 4 by 15 metres and recorded who broke the rule. Of 2,264 visitors, 17% lured the monkeys in the control condition, 7% where the arguments were given, z = 4.82, p < .001, and 7% where the question was asked, z = 4.82, p < .001. The two interventions did not differ, z = 0.09, p = .928, across the 1,013 visitors who saw one of them. Visitors given both signs broke the rule more often, at 11%, than visitors given the question alone, z = 2.12, p < .05. A questionnaire at the exit reached 350 visitors. Asking the question raised how important the rule was rated, from 5.73 to 6.03 on a seven-point scale, F(1, 345) = 6.48, p < .05, partial eta squared 0.018. Providing arguments did not, F(1, 345) = 0.69, p = .408. Damen, Müller, van Baaren and Dijksterhuis gave 120 Radboud University students either arguments for a clean local environment or the task of writing those arguments themselves. Neither the persuasion type nor a preceding manipulation of felt agency moved attitudes on its own, both F values below 1. The two interacted, F(1, 116) = 9.20, p = .003, partial eta squared 0.07, and generating the arguments beat receiving them only among students who had just been made to feel in control, F(1, 116) = 7.35, p = .008.

examples.tag: The safety briefing that asks for reasons
examples.text: Instead of listing why the guard rail matters, a supervisor asks each worker to say what could go wrong without it. The claim is about who produced the argument: a reason a worker states himself is meant to shift his behaviour more than the same reason on a laminated card.

examples.tag: The essay for the side you did not pick
examples.text: A tutor asks a student to write the strongest case for a policy she opposes. What is supposed to move her is not the content of the argument, which she could have read anywhere, but the fact that she assembled it.

examples.tag: The recruit who explains the rule
examples.text: A volunteer coordinator asks a new recruit to explain to the next intake why shifts start on time. The rule is unchanged and so are the reasons for it. The difference the claim rests on is that the recruit now spoke them.

replication.headline: Meta-analysis finds that advocating a behaviour, on its own, does not reliably beat doing nothing, while preregistered laboratory studies find an advantage over supplied arguments when generating them feels easy.
replication.detail: Priolo and colleagues meta-analysed 29 published and nine unpublished studies of induced hypocrisy, the two-step procedure in which people first advocate a desirable behaviour and then recall their own failures to follow it. The full procedure beat a control on intention, r = .35, 95% CI [.22, .46], across 19 studies, and on behaviour, r = .30, 95% CI [.10, .48], across ten. The advocacy step on its own did not beat a control on intention, r = .16, 95% CI [-.06, .36], across eight studies, nor on behaviour, r = .17, 95% CI [-.01, .35], across six. The full procedure did beat advocacy alone on intention across 16 studies, though trim and fill found that estimate inflated, and the authors settle on r = .25, 95% CI [.15, .34]. Recalling transgressions without advocating anything beat a control, r = .25, 95% CI [.08, .41], and adding advocacy to it changed nothing detectable, r = .18, 95% CI [-.04, .35], both across eight studies. Whether the procedure produced the discomfort the theory needs was inconclusive, r = .18, 95% CI [-.02, .36], across seven studies. Loman and colleagues showed 149 people an anti-alcohol poster framed either as an open question or as a statement, either briefly or throughout, then measured how much beer they drank in a taste test. The five groups did not differ, F(4, 140) = 0.76, p = .55, with a Bayes factor of 14.31 favouring the null over the model with condition in it. Xu and Wegener report five studies, two of them preregistered at 528 and 496 participants. Their abstract states that self-generated arguments beat other-generated arguments when people found generation easy, and that the advantage shrank when they found it hard. Catapano, Tormala and Rucker ran one experiment, a conceptual replication of it and a second experiment, 2,734 participants in all after exclusions. Taking an opponent's perspective before generating counter-attitudinal arguments cut attitude change, but only where the opponent's values differed. Against a control, the perspective of an opposed person of the same political leaning raised attitude change, t(1249) = 3.78, d = 0.24, while a different leaning cut it, t(1249) = 3.73, d = 0.28.

study.cite: Priolo, D., Pelt, A., St. Bauzel, R., Rubens, L., Voisin, D., & Fointiat, V. (2019). Three decades of research on induced hypocrisy: A meta-analysis. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 45(12), 1681-1701.

limits: The structured figure on this page is Priolo and colleagues' estimate for advocacy alone against a control, pooled over eight induced-hypocrisy studies. It is not a replication of any single experiment, it belongs to one procedure rather than to the family, and there is no matching original figure to set beside it. The authors did not test that comparison for publication bias, because the advocacy-only condition was not what the papers they pooled set out to measure. They did test the hypocrisy against advocacy comparison and found it inflated, which is why the corrected figure is the one given above. All their pooled figures were read from the accepted manuscript deposited at HAL rather than from the published article, and the two were not compared. Janis and King's 1954 paper, King and Janis's 1956 follow-up and Greenwald and Albert's 1968 paper were all read from Internet Archive scans of the bound journal volumes, a route no index lists. Aronson's 1999 article stays shut: it is closed at the publisher and open nowhere indexed by Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar or Europe PMC, checked on 21 September 2026, and the Internet Archive holds only a video lecture of the same title. Nothing on this page comes from it. Xu and Wegener's article is closed at Sage with no repository copy at any of those four indexes, and its result is taken from the publisher's abstract at Crossref. Higgins and Rholes's 1978 paper was not read here either, and is handled at entry no. 322. Catapano and colleagues' abstract calls their studies three preregistered experiments; the paper itself numbers two and reports the third as a conceptual replication of the first. Lemmen and colleagues assigned conditions to mornings rather than to individual visitors, and the observers watched unobtrusively while dressed as visitors. Their questionnaire reached 350 people, a seventh of the number observed, and 349 of those entered the analysis. Loman and colleagues used a forced taste test and raise the loss of free choice as a reason their posters may have done nothing. Damen and colleagues' 120 students are split four ways, so each cell holds about 30. No preregistered direct replication of Janis and King was located in a search on 21 September 2026 covering Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, the Internet Archive and web search.
misreadings: The first misreading is that self-persuasion is a mechanism. It names a procedure, and dissonance is one candidate explanation of why the procedure might work. The second is that the advocacy step is what does the work. In the hypocrisy literature that step alone did not beat a control, while recalling one's own failures did, and Priolo and colleagues recommend keeping both steps to make the normative standard salient rather than because advocacy carries the effect. The third is that beating a do-nothing control demonstrates anything about self-persuasion. Lemmen and colleagues' question sign cut rule-breaking from 17% to 7%, and so did the sign that simply gave the reasons, by the same amount. The fourth is that more is better, which overstates a result this page used to print flat. Visitors who got the arguments and then the question broke the rule more often than visitors who got the question alone, but against the arguments alone the same comparison reached only p = .052. The fifth is that the founding paper found the effect on everything it measured. Janis and King found it on two of their three topics. The phrase "saying is believing" also titles Higgins and Rholes's 1978 paper, which is about tuning a description to an audience and then remembering it that way, and is a different claim with its own entry, no. 322.
